summary: Standing observation tower in Watoga State Park, WV; one local article credits the CCC in the 1930s, an encyclopedia entry mentions an unnamed 1926 tower; climb status unstated.

facts.design: rustic lookout tower of American chestnut trees (one local article)
facts.agency: West Virginia Division of Natural Resources (manages Watoga State Park)

access.note: Reached by park trails; the sources do not say whether the tower itself is open to climb.

visit.trail_note: Ann Bailey Trail, 3 miles over Pyles Mountain and Workman Ridge, bikes allowed; a steep trail from Riverside Campground.

events.note: e-WV says a fire tower was erected at Watoga in 1926. It does not name the Ann Bailey lookout, so the link is unconfirmed.
Built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s, per the Pocahontas Times; no year given.

evidence.supports: listed as a standing observation tower in Pocahontas County
evidence.quote: Ann Bailey Pocahontas 38.10841 -80.16713 Obs Tower Standing

evidence.supports: park is in southern Pocahontas County
evidence.quote: The park is located in southern Pocahontas County on the Greenbrier River.

evidence.supports: Pocahontas Times article says the CCC built the lookout in the 1930s, using blight-infected American chestnut trees
evidence.quote: Built of blight-infected American chestnut trees by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s, this rustic lookout tower celebrates a warrior woman of the Revolutionary War period.

evidence.supports: two CCC camps set up in 1933 and 1934
evidence.quote: Two Civilian Conservation Corps camps were established, Camp Watoga in 1933 at the park's present maintenance area and Camp Seebert at the mouth of Island Lick Run in 1934.

evidence.supports: a third CCC camp opened in 1935
evidence.quote: A third CCC camp, Camp Will Rogers, was opened in 1935.

evidence.supports: park opened to the public on July 1, 1937
evidence.quote: Watoga State Park was opened to the public on July 1, 1937.

evidence.supports: a fire tower was erected at the park in 1926, not named
evidence.quote: In 1926, a fire tower was erected.

evidence.supports: the tower honors Ann Bailey, a warrior woman of the Revolutionary War period
evidence.quote: celebrates a warrior woman of the Revolutionary War period

evidence.supports: Ann Bailey's fame rests on an act that began at Fort Lee in 1791
evidence.quote: The act of supreme courage that made Ann Bailey famous for all time began in Fort Lee in 1791.

evidence.supports: the fort was about to run out of gunpowder
evidence.quote: it was discovered that, much like what happened in the story of Betty Zane, the fort would soon run out of gunpowder.

evidence.supports: the closest supply was in Lewisburg
evidence.quote: The closest source was in Lewisburg.

evidence.supports: Ann Bailey Trail is 3 miles and follows an old roadbed over Pyles Mountain and Workman Ridge
the Ann Bailey Trail welcomes mountain bikes and reaches the tower
evidence.quote: Trail follows the old roadbed across the top of Pyles Mountain and Workman Ridge to the Ann Bailey Lookout Tower. Mountain bikes welcome.

evidence.supports: a steep trail from Riverside Campground leads up to the tower
evidence.quote: The steep trail leading up to the Ann Bailey Lookout Tower offers spectacular views of the Greenbrier River Valley and Little Levels section of Pocahontas County.

evidence.supports: the Arrowhead trailhead is at Riverside Campground
evidence.quote: Trailhead is at Riverside Campground across from the check-in station.

evidence.supports: the Ann Bailey Lookout Tower is reached by pathways in Watoga State Park
evidence.quote: Many pathways will lead you toward the Ann Bailey Lookout Tower for stunning views over the Greenbrier Valley.

evidence.supports: the West Virginia Division of Natural Resources manages the park, and the park office keeps the trail map
evidence.quote: WVDNR manages Watoga, and the park office holds the trail map.

evidence.supports: the guide says to ask whether the structure is open to climb
evidence.quote: Ask which trails are signed toward the tower, how far it is from the parking you plan to use, and whether the structure is open to climb.

evidence.supports: the guide says to phone the park office before a visit
evidence.quote: Call the Watoga State Park office for the trail map and current signage before you plan the day.

notes_for_editor: Build date conflict left open: e-WV says a fire tower was erected at Watoga in 1926 (unnamed); the Pocahontas Times says the CCC built the Ann Bailey lookout in the 1930s. The construction material and the naming rest on one local article. Not used: grokipedia.com (unvetted encyclopedia copy claiming 1935 and CCC Company 1525), eathealthy365.com (claims a 1970s restoration; no primary source), and a WPA state files PDF on archive.org (text did not extract; its naming passage was seen only in a search snippet). A guessed westlookouts.weebly.com page returned 404. Whether the tower can be climbed is unknown; call the park before any visit. The West Virginia Outside post says WVDNR publishes no length for the Ann Bailey route, but the official trails page lists the Ann Bailey Trail at 3 miles; the story uses the official page. Two web searches used.
